Only eval 1 (automation-planning) is quantitatively discriminating -- evals 0 and 2 score 100% for both configurations because a strong baseline model already knows fintech test-strategy and release-gating conventions well. This doesn't mean the skill adds no value on those two evals: qualitatively, with_skill is more procedurally rigorous (explicit gate/phase checklists tied verbatim to SKILL.md, refusal to fabricate an unverified pass-rate figure) but the current assertions don't capture that distinction numerically.

The clearest, most reproducible skill value shown is in automation-planning: the skill's Phase 2 guidance (2automation.md) explicitly requires a three-way automate-now/automate-later/keep-manual decision and a flaky-test policy. The baseline defaulted to 'automate everything' and had zero flaky-test governance -- both are concrete, named parts of the skill that a general-purpose baseline had no way to reproduce.

with_skill runs took ~1.6x longer and used ~29% more tokens on average, mostly because they explicitly work through the skill's phase deliverables checklists and call out unmet gates -- a reasonable and expected cost of the extra rigor, not inefficiency.

In execution-reporting-under-pressure, the without_skill run computed and headlined a precise-looking '91% pass rate' derived from an unstated assumption, while with_skill explicitly refused to compute a number from insufficient data. No current assertion catches this; recommend adding one in a future iteration (e.g., 'does not present an unverified/assumed statistic as a precise, confidence-inspiring number without equal prominence given to the caveat').
